mainTopic: Whose understanding governs an oath, משה's oath wording, and the exaggerated vow about a snake like an olive-press beam
overview: The amud opens with רב אשי's answer that an oath follows the plain, common meaning of its words, so we never imagine a person secretly meant ants. The גמרא challenges this from the court's warning before an oath: 'we make you swear by our understanding, not by a condition in your heart.' It answers that the warning blocks a trick like the cane of רבא, where a borrower hid coins in a cane and handed it to the lender while swearing he had paid. A second challenge comes from משה, who made ישראל swear 'by my understanding and God's.' The גמרא answers that this blocks a real second meaning of a word: an idol can truly be called אלוה. It then asks why משה didn't pick a clearer oath wording, and tests several, from מצוות to תורה כולה. Each can be read narrowly until '613 מצוות' is suggested. The final answer is that משה simply chose a wording that was easy on the people. The amud ends with the משנה's exaggerated vow about a snake 'like the beam of an olive press,' which means a snake notched on its back. That wording also teaches that a real olive-press beam must be notched, which matters for sales.

steps.title: An oath follows the ordinary meaning of the words
steps.stepSummary: רב אשי answers that a person's oath is understood the way ordinary people understand it, so we do not imagine he secretly meant ants.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to him: When a person swears, he swears based on our common understanding. We do not even consider the idea that he meant ants.
steps.whatsHappening: רב אשי is answering a question: maybe a person who swore 'as many as left מצרים' secretly meant ants. He says no, an oath follows the plain meaning everyone understands.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The worry was that the oath might be true in some hidden sense, since there really are that many ants. רב אשי says the words of an oath are judged by normal human understanding, not by a strange private meaning. So the oath is read as being about people, the way anyone would hear it.

keyTerms.meaning: we do not even entertain the thought

phrases.english: He said to him: When he swears,
phrases.notes: This is רב אשי answering the worry that the person might have secretly meant ants.

phrases.english: he swears based on our understanding,
and we do not bring ourselves to think of ants.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲמַר לֵיהּ: כִּי מִשְׁתְּבַע אַדַּעְתָּא דִידַן מִשְׁתְּבַע
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the earlier question (from before this section) that the person might have meant ants.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Defines whose understanding governs an oath: the common one, not a hidden private meaning.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The oath might be true because the swearer privately meant ants, which are truly that numerous.
steps.terutzMaskana: An oath is judged by ordinary human understanding, so it refers to people.

steps.title: Challenge from the court's warning before an oath
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks whether a person really never swears by his own private meaning, and brings a ברייתא where the court warns him not to rely on a hidden condition in his heart.
steps.simpleTranslation: Does a person not swear according to his own understanding? But a ברייתא teaches: When the court makes someone swear, they tell him: Know that we are not making you swear based on a condition in your heart, but based on our understanding and the understanding of the court.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא pushes back on רב אשי by quoting a ברייתא about the warning the court gives before an oath. This sets up a question the גמרא will develop in the next steps.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רב אשי said oaths simply follow common understanding. But if that were automatic, why would the court need to warn the person that it is not his private meaning that counts? The warning hints that people do sometimes swear with their own private meaning in mind.

keyTerms.meaning: make someone swear / administer an oath
according to the understanding of the court

phrases.english: And according to his own understanding,
does a person not swear?
But it was taught: When they make him swear,
they say to him: Know
that not based on a condition in your heart
are we making you swear,
but rather based on our understanding
and based on the understanding of the court.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְעַל דַּעְתָּא דְנַפְשֵׁיהּ לָא עֲבִיד אִינִישׁ דְּמִשְׁתְּבַע? וְהָתַנְיָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges רב אשי's claim that oaths automatically follow common understanding.
steps.kashyaTarget: רב אשי's statement that a person swears based on our understanding.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The court must warn people not to rely on private meaning, which suggests private meaning would otherwise count.

steps.title: What trick is the court's warning meant to block?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks what the warning excludes, and suggests it excludes someone who calls game tokens 'coins' in his mind.
steps.simpleTranslation: What does this exclude? Doesn't it exclude a case where he gave them game tokens, and in his mind gave them the name 'coins'?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks what kind of trick the court's warning is trying to stop. It suggests the case of a person who privately calls game tokens 'coins' so that he can swear he 'paid the coins.'
steps.deeperAnalysis: If the borrower gave back only worthless tokens but privately thinks of them as 'coins,' his oath 'I paid the coins' is true only in his private meaning. The ברייתא's warning would be needed to block exactly this. This sets up the full challenge in the next step.

keyTerms.meaning: what does it come to exclude?

phrases.english: What does it exclude?
Is it not to exclude where he gave them tokens
and gave them the name 'coins'?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Clarifies what the ברייתא's warning is aimed at, building the challenge.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Which trick the court's warning about private conditions is designed to exclude.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: Suggested: someone privately calling game tokens 'coins.'

steps.title: So people do swear by their own private meaning
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא concludes its challenge: since the court had to say 'by our understanding,' people must normally swear by their own understanding.
steps.simpleTranslation: And since it says 'by our understanding,' that implies a person does swear according to his own understanding!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא finishes the challenge against רב אשי. The very need for the warning shows people usually swear by their own meaning.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Steps 2 and 3 gathered the pieces; this step states the attack openly. If private meaning never counted, the court would not need to say 'by our understanding.' So, against רב אשי, private meaning seems to matter unless the court excludes it.

phrases.english: And since it says 'by our understanding,'
this implies that a person does
swear according to his own understanding!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Completes the challenge built in steps 2 and 3.
steps.kashyaTarget: רב אשי's rule that oaths follow common understanding.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The warning 'by our understanding' would be pointless unless people normally swear by their own private meaning.

steps.title: The warning targets a different trick: the cane of רבא
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers that the court's warning is not about private word meanings but about a trick like the one in the story of 'the cane of רבא.'
steps.simpleTranslation: No, it comes to exclude a case like the cane of רבא.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא rejects the idea that the warning is about tokens called 'coins.' It says the warning is aimed at a different kind of trick, and it is setting up a story to explain it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If the warning is about some other trick, then it proves nothing about people swearing by private meanings. That saves רב אשי's rule. What the 'cane of רבא' trick was is explained in the story that follows.

phrases.english: No, it is to exclude the case of the cane of רבא.
phrases.notes: This refers to a well-known case before רבא, told right after this.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of step 4 by reassigning what the warning excludes.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Reinterprets what the ברייתא's warning is aimed at.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The warning excludes private word meanings, like calling tokens 'coins.'
steps.terutzMaskana: The warning excludes a trick like the cane of רבא, so רב אשי's rule stands.

steps.title: The story begins: a borrower claims he already paid
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא starts telling the story: a lender sued a borrower before רבא, the borrower said he paid, and רבא told him to swear that he paid.
steps.simpleTranslation: A certain man was owed money by another. He came before רבא. He said to the borrower: Go pay me. The borrower said: I already paid you. רבא said to him: If so, go swear to him that you paid him.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא begins the story of the cane of רבא to show what kind of trick the court's warning blocks. The story continues after this point.
steps.deeperAnalysis: So far the setup is simple: a debt, a claim of payment, and רבא requiring an oath. This sets the stage for the trick the borrower will try with his oath. The details of that trick come in the next part of the story.

keyTerms.meaning: was owed money by his fellow

phrases.aramaic: דְּהָהוּא גַּבְרָא דַּהֲוָה מַסֵּיק בְּחַבְרֵיהּ זוּזֵי,
phrases.english: For a certain man was owed money by his fellow,
he came before רבא.

phrases.aramaic: אֲמַר לֵיהּ לְלֹוֶה: זִיל פְּרַע לִי.
phrases.english: He said to the borrower: Go pay me.
He said to him: I paid you.
רבא said to him: If so,
go swear to him that you paid him.

steps.triggerLanguage: דְּהָהוּא גַּבְרָא דַּהֲוָה מַסֵּיק בְּחַבְרֵיהּ זוּזֵי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Begins telling the story referred to in step 5.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: When a borrower claims he already paid, רבא has him swear that he paid.

steps.title: The borrower hides coins in a cane and swears
steps.stepSummary: The borrower puts coins inside a hollow cane, hands it to the lender while he swears, and swears he has repaid everything.
steps.simpleTranslation: The borrower went and brought a hollow cane, put coins inside it, and came to court leaning on it. He said to the lender: 'Hold this cane for me.' Then he took a ספר תורה and swore that he had repaid all that was in his hand.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא continues the story of the cane of רבא. It shows the borrower's sneaky plan to make a false-sounding oath technically true.
steps.deeperAnalysis: While the lender holds the cane, the money really is in the lender's hands at that moment. So when the borrower swears 'I paid you,' it is technically true. His plan is to take the cane back right after the oath.

keyTerms.meaning: a cane (here, a hollow walking stick)
a Torah scroll, held while taking an oath

phrases.english: He went and brought a cane,
phrases.notes: 'He' is the borrower from the previous step.

phrases.english: and put coins inside it,

phrases.aramaic: וַהֲוָה מִסְתְּמִיךְ וְאָזֵיל וְאָתֵי עֲלֵיהּ לְבֵי דִּינָא.
phrases.english: and he was leaning on it as he came to the court.
He said to the lender:
Hold this cane in your hand.
He took a Torah scroll
and swore that he had repaid him
all that was his in his hand.
phrases.notes: Literally 'all that he had in his hand.' Right now the lender is holding all the money, hidden inside the cane.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the story begun in step 6, after רבא told the borrower to swear.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The borrower arranged for the lender to hold the money-filled cane during the oath, so 'I repaid you' would be technically true.

steps.title: The cane breaks and the coins spill out
steps.stepSummary: The angry lender breaks the cane, the coins fall out, and it becomes clear the oath was technically true.
steps.simpleTranslation: The lender got angry and broke the cane. The coins spilled onto the ground, and it turned out the borrower had sworn the truth.
steps.whatsHappening: The story ends. The trick is exposed when the lender smashes the cane in anger.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The lender thought he had just heard a false oath, so he broke the cane in frustration. The spilled coins showed that, in a narrow sense, the oath was true. This is the kind of trick the court blocks by saying 'you swear by our understanding,' as step 5 explained.

keyTerms.meaning: it turned out, it was found

steps.whatToRemember: The court's warning, 'swear by our understanding,' is aimed at tricks like the cane of רבא. Words can be technically true and still deceive. In step 5 the גמרא said the warning is about this, not about private meanings of words.
steps.confusionAlert: Don't think the borrower was honest because 'he swore the truth.' The oath was only technically true. He meant to take the cane and the money back right after the oath.

phrases.english: That lender got angry
and broke that cane,
and those coins spilled onto the ground,
and it turned out that he had sworn the truth.

steps.triggerLanguage: הָהוּא מַלְוֶה רְגַז וְתַבְרֵהּ לְהָהוּא קַנְיָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Finishes the story from step 7 and shows the trick that the answer in step 5 relies on.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The oath was technically true but deceptive. Such tricks are why the court has the oath taken by its own understanding.

steps.title: A new challenge from משה's oath in ערבות מואב
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks again whether people really don't swear by their own meaning, and brings a ברייתא where משה warns ישראל that they swear by his understanding and God's.
steps.simpleTranslation: Is it still true that a person doesn't swear by his own understanding? But a ברייתא teaches: When משה רבינו made ישראל swear in ערבות מואב, he told them: 'Know that I am not making you swear by your understanding, but by my understanding and God's,' as the פסוק says: 'And not with you alone...'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא reopens its challenge with a new source. It quotes a ברייתא about משה, and the next steps will spell out the argument.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The cane story answered the first source, but the גמרא now finds another warning like it. משה also had to say 'not by your understanding.' This hints that people might otherwise swear by their own private meaning.

keyTerms.meaning: the plains of מואב, where משה spoke before his death

phrases.english: And still, does a person not
swear by his own understanding?
But it was taught in a ברייתא:
And so we found with משה our teacher
when he made Israel swear in the plains of Moav,
he said to them: Know

phrases.aramaic: שֶׁלֹּא עַל דַּעְתְּכֶם אֲנִי מַשְׁבִּיעַ אֶתְכֶם,
phrases.english: that I am not making you swear by your understanding,

phrases.aramaic: אֶלָּא עַל דַּעְתִּי וְעַל דַּעַת הַמָּקוֹם,
phrases.english: but by my understanding and by the understanding of God,
as it says: "And not with you alone, etc."

steps.triggerLanguage: וְאַכַּתִּי לָא עֲבִיד דְּמִישְׁתְּבַע אַדַּעְתָּא דְנַפְשֵׁיהּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: After the cane story answered the first challenge, the גמרא brings a second source with the same kind of warning.
steps.kashyaTarget: The claim that a person never swears by his own private meaning, which the answer in step 5 defended.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: If משה had to warn ישראל not to swear by their own understanding, people must sometimes do so. The cane-trick answer may not fit this case.

steps.title: What was משה really warning about?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא explains משה's warning: he was afraid ישראל would sin and claim they swore 'by our understanding.'
steps.simpleTranslation: What was משה telling ישראל? Wasn't he saying: 'Maybe you will do sins and say, we swore by our own understanding.' That's why he said: 'By my understanding.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא explains what משה's warning meant. This sets up the next step, which pins down exactly what it rules out.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The גמרא reads משה's words as blocking a future excuse. Someone might sin and say 'my oath meant something else to me.' This is the same pattern as step 3, where the גמרא asked what the court's warning comes to exclude.

phrases.english: What was משה telling Israel?
Isn't this what he was saying to them:
Perhaps you will do things,
phrases.notes: 'Things' here means sins, things the oath forbids.

phrases.english: and you will say: We swore by our own understanding.

phrases.aramaic: מִשּׁוּם הָכִי אֲמַר לְהוּ: עַל דַּעְתִּי.
phrases.english: Because of this he told them: By my understanding.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Explains the ברייתא quoted in step 9 to build the challenge.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: What was the purpose of משה's warning 'by my understanding'?
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: To stop ישראל from sinning later and excusing it with 'we swore by our own understanding.'

steps.title: The proof: people do swear by their own meaning
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא says משה's warning excludes calling an idol 'אלוה', so people must normally swear by their own understanding.
steps.simpleTranslation: What does this warning exclude? Doesn't it exclude people who give an idol the name 'God'? That shows a person does swear by his own understanding!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא finishes its challenge. It argues that משה's warning only makes sense if people normally swear by their own private meaning.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The case being excluded is someone who swears to serve 'אלוה' while privately meaning an idol. That is a private meaning of a word, not a cane-style trick. So the step 5 answer doesn't seem to fit here, and the challenge stands against the idea that people never swear by their own meaning.

keyTerms.meaning: they gave the name, they called
God (a name that could be misapplied to an idol)

steps.whatToRemember: משה's warning seems aimed at private meaning, calling an idol 'אלוה.' That is exactly what step 5 said the court's warning was NOT about. The next step answers this challenge.

phrases.english: To exclude what?
Isn't it to exclude
people who give an idol the name 'God'?
This shows that a person does
swear by his own understanding!

steps.triggerLanguage: לְאַפּוֹקֵי מַאי? לָאו לְאַפּוֹקֵי דְּאַסִּיקוּ שְׁמָא לַעֲבוֹדָה זָרָה אֱלוֹהַּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Completes the challenge built in steps 9-10, using the same 'what does it exclude' reasoning as steps 3-4.
steps.kashyaTarget: The answer of step 5, that such warnings only target tricks like the cane of רבא and never private meanings.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: משה's warning rules out a private meaning of a word (an idol called 'אלוה'). The warning would not be needed unless people do swear by their own understanding.

steps.title: An idol really is called אלוה
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא rejects the proof from Step 11. Calling an idol 'אלוה' is a real meaning of the word, not a private mental condition.
steps.simpleTranslation: No. An idol is also called 'אלוה', as it says: 'And against all the gods of Egypt…'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the challenge from Step 11. משה's warning does not prove that people normally swear by their own private understanding.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The proof in Step 11 assumed that ישראל would be relying on a private thought in their heads. But the תורה itself uses the word אלהים for idols, so 'אלוה' can honestly mean an idol. משה was blocking a real second meaning of the word. So the rule still stands that people do not swear by their own private meaning.

keyTerms.meaning: God; a word that can also refer to a false god

phrases.english: No, idol worship is called 'God',
as it is written: 'And against all the gods of Egypt, etc.'

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the קשיא of Step 11
steps.terutzResolutionType: Shows the second meaning is built into the word itself, not a private intention
steps.terutzHavaAmina: משה's warning proves people normally swear by their own private understanding
steps.terutzMaskana: The warning only blocks a real meaning of the word אלוה, so it proves nothing about private intentions
steps.whatToRemember: משה's warning was about a word that really has two meanings. It was not about private thoughts. So people still do not swear by their own hidden meaning.

steps.title: Why not simply swear to keep the מצוות?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks why משה did not just make them swear 'that you will keep the מצוות', which would include not worshipping idols.
steps.simpleTranslation: Let him make them swear: 'that you will keep the מצוות'!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks why משה needed his special warning at all. A broad oath about the מצוות would already cover idol worship.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If the oath covered all the מצוות, there would be no gap for the 'idol is אלוה' trick. This step opens a chain of suggested wordings, which ends in step 26.

phrases.english: But let him make them swear
that you will keep the מצוות!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges whether משה's special wording was needed
steps.kashyaTarget: The need for משה's warning 'by my understanding'
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: A general oath to keep the מצוות would already forbid idol worship, so the warning seems unnecessary

steps.title: 'מצוות' could mean the king's commands
steps.stepSummary: The word 'מצוות' could be read as the commands of a king, so it would not clearly mean God's מצוות.
steps.simpleTranslation: That would mean the commands of the king.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that 'מצוות' is not clear enough, because it can also mean a human king's orders.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A command from a king is also called a מצוה. Someone could swear to keep 'מצוות' while meaning only royal orders. So the word leaves the same kind of gap.

phrases.english: That could mean the commands of the king.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers Step 13
steps.terutzResolutionType: Shows the suggested word has a second, narrower meaning
steps.terutzHavaAmina: 'מצוות' clearly means all of God's מצוות
steps.terutzMaskana: 'מצוות' can also mean a king's commands

steps.title: Why not swear to keep ALL the מצוות?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא suggests adding the word 'all' so the oath clearly covers every מצוה.
steps.simpleTranslation: Let him make them swear: 'that you will keep all the מצוות'!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא tries a stronger wording. Adding 'all' should rule out the narrow 'king's commands' meaning.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The word 'all' seems to point to the complete set of the תורה's מצוות. So the gap from Step 14 looks closed.

phrases.english: But let him make them swear
that you will keep all the מצוות!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Builds on Step 14 by suggesting a fuller wording
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: 'All the מצוות' cannot be mistaken for a king's commands

steps.title: 'All the מצוות' could mean ציצית
steps.stepSummary: 'All the מצוות' could be read as ציצית alone, because ציצית is said to equal all the מצוות.
steps.simpleTranslation: That could mean the מצוה of ציצית, as the Master said: the מצוה of ציצית is equal to all the מצוות in the תורה.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that even 'all the מצוות' has a narrow meaning. It could refer to ציצית alone.
steps.deeperAnalysis: There is a known teaching that ציצית is weighed as equal to all the מצוות. So someone could swear 'all the מצוות' and mean only ציצית. The gap is still open.

phrases.english: That could mean the mitzvah of ציצית,
as the Master said:
The mitzvah of ציצית is equal
to all the מצוות in the Torah.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers Step 15
steps.terutzResolutionType: Uses a known teaching to show a narrower possible meaning
steps.terutzHavaAmina: 'All the מצוות' must mean every מצוה
steps.terutzMaskana: It could mean ציצית, which is counted as equal to all of them
steps.confusionAlert: The גמרא is not saying that ציצית replaces the other מצוות. It only says the phrase 'all the מצוות' could be understood as pointing to ציצית.

steps.title: Why not swear to keep the תורה?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא suggests the oath wording 'that you will keep the תורה'.
steps.simpleTranslation: Let him make them swear: 'that you will keep the תורה'!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא tries another wording that seems to cover everything: the whole תורה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: 'תורה' seems to sidestep both earlier problems. It cannot mean a king's orders, and it cannot mean ציצית alone.

keyTerms.meaning: Torah; also 'a law' or 'a set of rules'

phrases.english: But let him make them swear that you will keep the Torah!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Proposes a new wording after Step 16
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: 'Torah' seems to cover everything without the narrow meanings of 'מצוות'

steps.title: 'Torah' means only one תורה
steps.stepSummary: 'תורה' in the singular means only one תורה, not both.
steps.simpleTranslation: That means only one תורה.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that 'תורה' in the singular leaves something out, because it points to just one תורה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: There is more than one תורה: תורה שבכתב and תורה שבעל פה. A singular word could be read as covering only one of them, so the oath would not be complete.

phrases.english: That means: one Torah.
phrases.notes: He means only the written Torah, leaving out the oral Torah.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers Step 17
steps.terutzResolutionType: Points out that the singular form is too narrow

steps.title: Why not swear to keep the תורות?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא suggests the plural, 'תורות', so that both תורות are included.
steps.simpleTranslation: Let him make them swear: 'that you will keep the Torahs'!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא fixes the singular problem from Step 18 by using the plural.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The plural seems to cover both תורה שבכתב and תורה שבעל פה, which closes the gap from Step 18.

phrases.english: But let him make them swear that you will keep the Torahs!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Fixes the problem raised in Step 18
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The plural would include both Torahs

steps.title: 'Torahs' could mean the laws of certain offerings
steps.stepSummary: 'תורות' could mean the specific sets of laws for the מנחה, the חטאת and the אשם.
steps.simpleTranslation: That could mean the law of the מנחה, the law of the חטאת, the law of the אשם.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that the plural 'Torahs' can mean small sets of laws about particular קרבנות.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The תורה uses the word 'Torah' for the rules of a single offering, as in 'this is the Torah of the מנחה'. So 'Torahs' could mean just these few sets of offering laws, not the whole תורה.

phrases.english: That could mean: the law of the meal-offering,
phrases.notes: 'Torah' here means a set of rules, as in 'זאת תורת המנחה' (ויקרא 6:7).

phrases.english: the law of the sin-offering, the law of the guilt-offering.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers Step 19
steps.terutzResolutionType: Shows the plural word also has narrow technical meanings
steps.terutzHavaAmina: 'Torahs' means the written and oral Torah
steps.terutzMaskana: It could mean the laws of specific offerings

steps.title: Why not swear to keep the תורות and the מצוות?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא suggests combining both words, 'Torahs and מצוות'.
steps.simpleTranslation: Let him make them swear: 'that you will keep the Torahs and the מצוות'!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא tries one last wording that combines the two terms, hoping together they cover everything.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Each word alone had a narrow reading. Joining them might seem to make the oath complete.

phrases.english: But let him make them swear
that you will keep the Torahs and the מצוות!
phrases.notes: Some versions have the word in square brackets here and some don't.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Combines the wordings of Steps 13 and 19
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Two words together should cover what each one misses alone

steps.title: Each word still keeps its narrow meaning
steps.stepSummary: 'Torahs' could still mean the law of the מנחה, and 'מצוות' could still mean the king's commands, so this combined wording also leaves a gap.
steps.simpleTranslation: 'Torahs' could mean the law of the מנחה, and 'מצוות' could mean the king's commands.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that putting the two words together does not help, because each word can still be read narrowly. The גמרא will keep suggesting wordings in the next steps.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Joining two words that are each unclear does not make either one clear. The גמרא keeps looking for a clear wording in the next steps.

phrases.english: 'Torahs' could mean: the law of the meal-offering.
phrases.notes: Some versions have the word in square brackets here and some don't.

phrases.english: 'מצוות' could mean: the commands of the king.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers Step 21; the chain of suggested wordings continues in Step 23
steps.terutzResolutionType: Reuses the narrow meanings already given for each word
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Combining the words makes the oath cover everything
steps.terutzMaskana: Each word stays open to a narrow reading, so this combined wording also fails
steps.whatToRemember: Every simple wording so far (מצוות, all the מצוות, תורה, תורות, תורות and מצוות) can be read narrowly. Steps 23-25 keep searching, and in step 26 the גמרא admits that clearer wordings did exist.
steps.whyThisMatters: This shows how carefully an oath's words are judged. An oath follows what its words can honestly mean, so a word with a real second meaning leaves a loophole that has to be closed.

steps.title: Why not swear to keep the whole Torah?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא suggests that משה could have made the people swear to keep 'the whole Torah', which would be clear.
steps.simpleTranslation: Let him make them swear: 'that you will keep the whole Torah'!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא offers yet another wording that seems clear enough, so that משה would not need his special warning.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Earlier wordings like 'תורה', 'תורות' or 'מצוות' could be twisted. 'תורה כולה' seems impossible to twist, because 'whole' leaves nothing out.

keyTerms.meaning: And let him make them swear

phrases.english: And let him make them swear
that you will keep the whole Torah!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Proposes a new, broader wording after 'Torahs and מצוות' was shown to be twistable.
steps.kashyaTarget: The claim that משה needed to say 'according to my understanding and the understanding of the המקום'.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: 'The whole Torah' seems to cover everything with no room for a twisted reading.

steps.title: 'The whole Torah' can mean just idol worship
steps.stepSummary: 'The whole Torah' could be read as only rejecting עבודה זרה, because a ברייתא says that whoever rejects idols is like someone who accepts the whole Torah.
steps.simpleTranslation: 'The whole Torah' can mean idol worship, as a ברייתא teaches: idol worship is so serious that anyone who rejects it is as if he accepts the whole Torah.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that even 'the whole Torah' could be twisted, and it brings a ברייתא to show how.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Because rejecting עבודה זרה is called 'like accepting the whole Torah', the people could claim they only swore not to worship idols. So this wording still leaves a loophole.

phrases.english: 'The whole Torah' can mean: idol worship.
As it was taught: idol worship is so serious
that anyone who rejects it
is as if he accepts the whole Torah.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Shows that the wording suggested in step 23 can also be twisted.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Reinterpretation of the phrase, supported by a ברייתא
steps.terutzHavaAmina: 'The whole Torah' clearly includes every מצוה.
steps.terutzMaskana: 'The whole Torah' can be used as a name for rejecting עבודה זרה alone, so it is still open to a twisted reading.

steps.title: Why not say idol worship plus the whole Torah, or 613 מצוות?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא suggests combining 'idol worship and the whole Torah', or simply saying '613 מצוות'.
steps.simpleTranslation: Let him make them swear 'that you will keep idol worship and the whole Torah', or else '613 מצוות'!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא offers two more wordings that really cannot be twisted.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If עבודה זרה is listed separately, 'the whole Torah' can no longer mean just idol worship. A number like 613 also leaves no room for a twisted reading at all.

phrases.english: And let him make them swear that you will keep
idol worship and the whole Torah,
phrases.notes: 'Keep idol worship' means keep the מצוה of staying away from it.

phrases.aramaic: אִי נָמֵי: שֵׁשׁ מֵאוֹת וּשְׁלֹשׁ עֶשְׂרֵה מִצְוֹת!
phrases.english: or else: six hundred and thirteen מצוות!

steps.triggerLanguage: וְלַישְׁבַּע יָתְהוֹן דִּמְקַיְּימִיתוּן עֲבוֹדָה זָרָה וְתוֹרָה כּוּלָּהּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Fixes the loophole found in step 24 by adding עבודה זרה separately, or by counting the מצוות.
steps.kashyaTarget: The need for משה's special phrase 'according to my understanding'.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: These wordings close every loophole, so a simpler clear wording was available.

steps.title: משה chose an easy wording
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא concludes that משה רבינו chose wording that would not burden the people.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, משה רבינו used a simple expression that was not troublesome.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא admits that clearer wordings existed. It explains that משה picked a simple, easy way instead.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The answer no longer claims that every wording can be twisted. It says משה preferred not to burden the people with long or complicated oaths, so he used a short oath plus 'according to my understanding'.

keyTerms.meaning: A matter that is not troublesome

steps.whatToRemember: משה's special oath 'according to my understanding and the understanding of the המקום' closed every loophole in a simple way. Any wording the people might twist was covered, without a burdensome oath.

phrases.english: Rather, Moshe our teacher
used an expression that was not troublesome.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֶלָּא, מֹשֶׁה רַבֵּינוּ מִילְּתָא דְּלָא טְרִיחָא נְקַט
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Accepts the point of step 25 but explains why משה still chose his own method.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: משה used his special warning only because no clear wording existed.
steps.terutzMaskana: Clear wordings did exist, but משה chose the easiest way that still left no loophole.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: משה's oath format was a choice of simplicity, not a necessity.

steps.title: Huge snakes really exist
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes the משנה's exaggerated vow about a snake like an olive-press beam. It challenges this, since a snake in the days of שבור מלכא swallowed thirteen bundles of straw.
steps.simpleTranslation: The משנה said: 'If I did not see a snake like the beam of an olive press.' And is there no such snake? But there was a snake in the days of King שבור that was thrown thirteen bundles of straw and swallowed them!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא moves to a new topic in the משנה. It challenges why seeing a snake as big as a beam counts as a נדר הבאי (an exaggerated vow).
steps.deeperAnalysis: A נדר הבאי is not binding because everyone knows the speaker is exaggerating. But if such big snakes really exist, the statement might be true, so it should not count as an exaggeration.

keyTerms.meaning: The beam of an olive press

phrases.english: 'If I did not see a snake
like the beam of an olive press.'
phrases.notes: This is quoted from the משנה's list of vows that are clearly exaggerations.

phrases.english: And is there not such a snake?
But there was a certain snake
that lived in the days of King Shapur,
they threw it thirteen bundles of straw
and it swallowed them!

steps.triggerLanguage: אִם לֹא רָאִיתִי נָחָשׁ כְּקוֹרַת בֵּית הַבַּד, וְלָא? וְהָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new topic: the משנה's example of an exaggerated vow.
steps.kashyaTarget: The משנה's classification of the snake vow as a נדר הבאי.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: A real snake that size exists, so the statement could be true and would not be an exaggeration.

steps.title: שמואל: 'Like the beam' means notched
steps.stepSummary: שמואל explains that the vow refers to a snake that is notched, like the notches of an olive-press beam.
steps.simpleTranslation: שמואל said: it is talking about a notched snake.
steps.whatsHappening: שמואל answers that the comparison to the beam is about its notched shape, not its size.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The beam of an olive press had notches or grooves. So the vow means 'a snake with notches like the beam', which makes the comparison about shape, not size. Why such a snake would be unbelievable is worked out in the next two steps.

phrases.english: Shmuel said: it is talking about a notched one.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers step 27 by shifting the comparison from size to shape.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: 'Like the beam' means as big as the beam.
steps.terutzMaskana: 'Like the beam' means notched like the beam.

steps.title: All snakes are notched
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא objects that every snake has notches, so a notched snake is nothing special.
steps.simpleTranslation: But all snakes are notched!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges שמואל's answer, since notches are normal on snakes.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If every snake has notches, then 'I saw a notched snake' is plainly true. It would not be an exaggeration either.

phrases.english: All snakes are notched!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Attacks שמואל's answer in step 28.
steps.kashyaTarget: שמואל's explanation that the snake was notched.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Notches are normal on all snakes, so seeing one is not an exaggeration.

steps.title: Notched on its back
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers that the vow refers to a snake notched on its back, which is not what snakes are like.
steps.simpleTranslation: We are talking about one notched on its back.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא sharpens שמואל's answer: the notches are on the snake's back, just like the beam.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Ordinary snakes are notched, but not on the back the way an olive-press beam is. Claiming to have seen a snake notched on its back is an exaggeration, so the vow is a נדר הבאי.

phrases.english: We are saying notched on its back.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Defends שמואל against step 29 by specifying where the notches are.
steps.terutzMaskana: Only a snake notched on its back, like the beam, which is an unbelievable claim.

steps.title: Why not just say 'notched'?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks why the משנה did not simply say 'a notched snake' instead of 'like the beam of an olive press'.
steps.simpleTranslation: Then let the משנה say 'notched'!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges the משנה's wording. If the point is notches, it could have said so directly.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Comparing the snake to a beam seems like a roundabout way to say 'notched'. The גמרא wants to know why the תנא chose this wording.

keyTerms.meaning: Then let him teach / say it

phrases.english: Then let it teach 'notched'?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Accepts the explanation in step 30 but questions the משנה's wording.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: If the meaning is 'notched', the beam comparison is unnecessary.

steps.title: Teaching a side lesson about the beam
steps.stepSummary: The משנה uses the beam comparison to teach, in passing, that an olive-press beam is notched on its back.
steps.simpleTranslation: It teaches us something along the way: the beam of an olive press is notched on its back.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא explains that the משנה chose this wording on purpose, to slip in an extra piece of information.
steps.deeperAnalysis: By saying 'like the beam', the משנה tells us what a proper olive-press beam looks like. A real one has a notched back.

keyTerms.meaning: A matter in passing / along the way

phrases.aramaic: מִילְּתָא אַגַּב אוֹרְחֵיהּ קָא מַשְׁמַע לַן,
phrases.english: It teaches us a matter in passing:
that the beam of an olive press is notched on its back.

steps.triggerLanguage: מִילְּתָא אַגַּב אוֹרְחֵיהּ קָא מַשְׁמַע לַן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers step 31 by giving a reason for the משנה's wording.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Wording chosen to teach an extra point
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The beam comparison is extra wording.
steps.terutzMaskana: It teaches that an olive-press beam has a notched back.

steps.title: What difference does it make?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks what practical difference this fact about the beam makes.
steps.simpleTranslation: What practical difference does this make?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks why we need to know that the beam is notched. This sets up the next answer.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Facts about tools only matter in a משנה if they affect הלכה. The גמרא looks for the practical result.

keyTerms.meaning: What practical difference does it make?

phrases.english: What difference does it make?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks for the purpose of the side lesson in step 32.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: The halachic result of knowing that an olive-press beam is notched.

steps.title: It matters for buying and selling
steps.stepSummary: If someone sells an 'olive-press beam', the sale is valid only if the beam has a notched back.
steps.simpleTranslation: It matters for buying and selling. If someone sells an olive-press beam to his friend: if its back is notched, the sale is good; if not, it is not.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives the practical result: it defines what counts as an olive-press beam in a sale.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A buyer who pays for an 'olive-press beam' expects the real thing. A beam without notches is not called by that name, so selling one under that name is not a valid sale.
steps.whatToRemember: 'Like the beam of an olive press' means a snake notched on its back, which is an impossible claim, so the vow is a נדר הבאי. The wording also teaches that a true olive-press beam is notched, which matters for sales.

phrases.english: For buying and selling,
to tell you:
one who sells the beam of an olive press to his friend,
if its back is notched, yes,
and if not, no.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 33.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The fact defines what an 'olive-press beam' is in a sale: only a notched-back beam qualifies.
